what_its_for: Infliximab-Abda is used to treat several conditions where your immune system attacks your own body. These include rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis, and plaque psoriasis. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF-alpha that causes inflammation and can damage your joints, skin, and digestive tract.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV (intravenous) infusion directly into your vein at a clinic, hospital, or infusion center. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. A trained healthcare provider will slowly drip the medicine into your bloodstream over at least 2 hours. You will be watched closely during and after the infusion for any reactions. Plan to be at the infusion center for several hours on each visit.
dosing: Your dose depends on your weight and the condition being treated. For most conditions, you will receive an infusion at week 0, week 2, and week 6, and then every 6 to 8 weeks after that. Your doctor will calculate the exact dose in milligrams per kilogram of your body weight. Never try to adjust your own dose — always follow your doctor's instructions exactly.
missed_dose: If you miss or have to reschedule an infusion appointment, contact your doctor or infusion center as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your doctor will advise you on the best time to reschedule your next infusion to keep your treatment on track.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the infusion center. You do not need to store it at home. If you are given any supplies related to your treatment, store them in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze. Keep all supplies away from children and out of direct sunlight.
what_to_avoid: Avoid being around people who are sick or have infections, as this medicine lowers your immune system and makes it harder for your body to fight infections. Do not receive live vaccines (such as the live flu nasal spray, MMR, chickenpox, or shingles vaccine Zostavax) while on this medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid smoking, as it can make your condition worse. Tell all of your doctors and dentists that you are on this medicine before any procedures.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have: signs of infection such as fever, chills, cough, or burning when you urinate; chest pain or trouble breathing; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, rash, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty swallowing; unusual bruising or bleeding; numbness or tingling in your hands or feet; vision changes; or signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or severe stomach pain. Also call your doctor if you notice any new or unusual lumps, as this medicine may rarely increase the risk of certain cancers.
when_it_works: Some people begin to feel better within a few weeks, but it may take several months to feel the full benefit of this medicine. It is important to keep all of your infusion appointments even if you do not notice improvement right away. Do not stop treatment without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you receive this medicine during pregnancy, your baby may be at higher risk of infection for up to 6 months after birth. Newborns exposed to this medicine in the womb should not receive live vaccines until they are at least 6 months old. Children: This medicine can be used in children 6 years and older for Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Older adults: Older patients may have a higher risk of serious infections while on this medicine. Close monitoring is recommended. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver conditions you have before starting this medicine.
